agency: Department for Business, Energy and Industrial Strategy
titles: Praise Export Services Limited and Queen's University of Belfast
descriptions:
Development of a novel, rapid, non-destructive, handheld test to determine integrity and quality of red palm oil and palm cream concentrate.
Innovation area – Food integrity/authenticity
The KTP plan will deliver two tests, one to rapidly measure/validate the quality of palm oil and the other to check for Sudan dye adulteration. It will develop, validate and implement novel techniques that are rapid, low cost and reliable, using vibrational spectroscopy.
The Institute for Global Food Security are world-leading experts in such techniques and will work alongside researchers in Cape Coast University to successfully deliver the project. The outcome will be an industry based Quality Assurance Scheme that will be recognised by the government in Ghana and customers that import Ghanaian palm oil.
ODA – KTP will deliver benefit the company’s profitability, but also will benefit the entire workforce, providing opportunities for upskilling and training in new processing and analytical techniques. The KTP will have far reaching benefits across the local community. Livelihoods will be significantly improved in the farming communities particularly for women who constitute about 80% of the workforce, and who are employed along the value chain to strip the fruits for production of oil. There will also be opportunities to increase the workforce involved in the production of the oil due to the increased demand by the coming on board of the rapid test. We anticipate that the assurance received by global customers of the quality of Palm oil by this innovative technology would eventually double or triple the already huge demand for the product thereby resulting in the employment of more women on the farms and at the oil mills.
Oil Palm Farmers and mill operators who do not receive their monies for supplies made to aggregators under the pretext that the oils failed the Sudan dyes test and for that matter could not be sold, would now be able to authenticate their oils right on the farm or at the mills almost instantly without the usual delays for third party testing and then receive their pay, helping to improve the livelihoods of the farmer, their families and other dependants.

agency: Department for Business, Energy and Industrial Strategy
titles: ColdHubs Limited and Aston University
descriptions:
To develop a hybrid solar-powered off-grid pre-cooling storage system for smallholder farmers clusters in Nigeria to supplement existing cold rooms, minimize agro-food waste, improve cooling efficiency, increase farmers' income and drive business growth in ColdHubs.
Innovation area – Storage
The KTP will develop and roll out ColdHub pre-coolers (CHPC), which will incorporate a hybrid solar-powered pre-cooling storage system using a different refrigeration system based on vapour compression-absorption and advanced numerical modelling to optimise sizing of the solar PV panels. The CHPCs will be located in smallholder farmers clusters to reduce the temperature of produce from typically 27°C to 12 - 15°C close to the producer before transfer to the ColdHubs, where the temperature is reduced to 8 - 10°C for optimal storage. This will;
a. Protect the quality (and value) of the produce by reducing spoilage in transit
b. Avoid overloading of the cold rooms, where the excess heat in the produce puts strain on the compressor based refrigeration in cooling from 27°C to 8 - 10°C
c. Extend produce shelf life from 2 to 21 days
ODA – the CHPCs will have an immediate impact on the income of smallholders in Nigeria by increasing the quantity of produce that reaches the markets / wholesalers due to the increased shelf life. ColdHubs project an increase in income from $60 to $120 per month is feasible, off-setting the additional costs of using the CHPCs.
There are over 93 million smallholder farmers in Nigeria, of which 70% are women, who will directly benefit from CHPCs as the technology as it rolls out across the country. agency: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
titles: ColdHubs Limited and Aston University
descriptions:
To develop a hybrid solar-powered off-grid pre-cooling storage system for smallholder farmers clusters in Nigeria to supplement existing cold rooms, minimize agro-food waste, improve cooling efficiency, increase farmers' income and drive business growth in ColdHubs.
Innovation area – Storage

The CHPCs will be located in smallholder farmers clusters to reduce the temperature of produce from typically 27°C to 12 - 15°C close to the producer before transfer to the ColdHubs, where the temperature is reduced to 8 - 10°C for optimal storage. agency: Department for Business, Energy and Industrial Strategy
titles: Farmtrack Consulting Limited and University of the West of Scotland
descriptions:
To develop a novel and environmentally friendly female fruit fly protein baited trap using locally available raw materials; to enhance supply chains (mangoes); and to address a key global food production challenge and contribute towards both societal and economic impact within Kenya and Africa.
Innovation area – Pest control
It is anticipated that 3 new full-time jobs and 20 casual jobs will be delivered from this project. In addition, 16 new jobs will be delivered within 5 years post KTP. Seven employees of the company will develop new skills in areas including: supply chain management, logistics, downstream production & product commercialisation, adding to streamlined operations and systems.
ODA – In Kenya, rural poverty is estimated at 38.8% (World Bank: Kenya Economic Update 2018). Studies suggest that use of traps in place of synthetic pesticides reduces household expenditure by 46.3%.The use of traps can increase rural household income by 22.4%-48%. The technology will enable farmers to produce higher volumes of marketable fruits, generate higher prices, contribute to nutritional security, and reduce insecticide expenditure. The new product, due to its high effectiveness/low labour costs, and 30% of the extra income being ploughed back into production, will add to fruit production sustainability and higher yields. The product will be developed from a natural corn based proteins by-product.
Since corn is a major staple food crop in Kenya this will not exert pressure on production systems to provide raw materials, thereby reducing carbon emissions. (Kenya National Bureau of Statistics (KNBS) Economic Survey 2019). There will be no runoff into water systems, no accumulation of pesticides in the food chain, and no environmental contamination. Current crop losses due to fruit flies can be up to 100% without interventions. The novel technology will reduce this wastage by 80% in the first three years after adoption and add 10% disposable income to farmers.
Invasion of fruits in Kenya by fruit flies has caused the production of low-grade fruits leading to banning of export to European Union countries and the USA. Smallholder farmers the majority of whom live below the poverty line produce mango. Losses due to the fruit fly can be as high as 100%. The development of a sustainably managed product will result in production of high grade fruits and higher prices in export markets thereby improving the livelihoods of poor farmers.

agency: Department for Business, Energy and Industrial Strategy
titles: Eco Fuels Kenya (EFK)POst harvest crop and University of Greenwich
descriptions:
To design and develop plant-based natural product innovations using Croton seed oil and the by-products from its extraction for sustainable, organic agriculture in Kenya that reduces farmer reliance on synthetic chemical pesticides and increases revenue for the farmers and the KTP business partner.
Innovation area – Pest control
Croton oil is extracted as a biofuel from Croton seeds and remains EFKs primary source of revenue. However, it is our strategic aim to commercialise Croton seed oil and by-products of its extraction into a wider product range, especially sustainable pest control. African farming is reliant on synthetic pesticides that have negative environmental and health impacts, and limit export potential to EU owing to residue restrictions (2009 EU Sustainable Use Directive). In response, EFKs vision is to increase revenue using Croton for eco-friendly and sustainable agriculture.
Routes to diversifying our portfolio include a) extracts from seed kernels as organic pesticides and plant growth boosters b) use of the oil in plant-based organic pesticide formulations. However, the evidence on efficacy remains anecdotal at this stage and requires scientific validation to be able to correctly develop and market these products. EFK currently lack the expertise for this validation.
ODA – This project has several wider benefits. By helping EFK grow its business, this project will benefit EFK’s croton collector network by increasing farmer income. If EFK is able to scale as projected to collect 7000 tons per year, this injects over £1.0M of additional income to smallholder farmers. Also, by increasing its market share for organic agricultural products, EFKs products will help revitalize farms and aid farmers in engaging in climate-smart agricultural practices. One of the current barriers to proper fertilizer and pesticide use is that farmers lack the correct training to correctly utilize products often resulting in hazardous use, especially with chemical pesticides. This project will result in smallholder farmers engaging in safe usage of organic products benefitting both themselves and the consumers of their produce. Finally, Kenya’s agricultural sector is over-reliant on foreign imports. The new croton-pyrethrum product will result in a completed new and organic product that is tied to key Kenyan natural resources. Kenya was once the biggest producer of high quality pyrethrum. This project will help engage regrowing that industry as it continues to develop the croton as new supply chain. This project supports the growth and scale of a local Kenya organization in creating products that have direct local benefits.

agency: Department for Business, Energy and Industrial Strategy
titles: Anolei Women Camel Milk Co-operative Limited and University of Greenwich
descriptions:
The project titled, "Adding value to camel milk value chain in Northern Kenya" partners with Anolei Women Camel Milk Co-operative to strengthen capacity for new value-added products and enhance productivity in camel milk production, collection and marketing.
Innovation area – Value addition
The KTP project aligns with the Anolei Women Camel Milk Co-operative’s aims to strengthen the capacity and livelihood security of women milk traders, by diversifying from primarily raw milk production and collection to a host of demand-driven value-added products. However, frequent milk spoilage and limited market reach have led to significant income and opportunity losses. The co-operative has identified the needs to strengthen capacity, in post-production technologies and business practices, while being cautious against the repeated instances of male appropriation when small enterprises become more lucrative and formalised.
Recent research has shown that 2% of the total camel milk produced in Kenya gets to the urban markets, 10% in local markets and 38% domestic consumption, and rest 50% are lost at harvest or during postharvest handling. Majority of the losses takes place due to physiochemical and microbiological changes along the value chain. The proposed project will focus to reduce these losses by half at Anolei Women Camel Milk Co-operative within the project duration. Apart from management innovation, the technological interventions which the project intends to apply at the co-op include solar cooling and improved logistics. Moreover, the project will also focus to reduce the reliance on fossil fuels and incorporate renewable energy resources which will help reduce pollution.
ODA – The introduction of value-added products and enhanced nutrition and health of camel will result in a significant financial payback to the cooperative and associated wider pastoralist community. By the end of the project, the capacity of the women co-operative will be increased by 7%, and over the next 5 years after the project, it is expected to further expand by 15%.
Camel milk has a significant contribution towards livelihoods in the arid and semi-arid lands (ASALs) of Kenya. 83% area of Kenya falls under ASALs, and support one-third of its population. Subsistence pastoralists and smallholder farmers in ASALs experience and one of the highest poverty levels in the country with 74-97% people living below the poverty line.
Camel milk contributes up to 40% of the pastoralist household income. Enhancing the safety and market for camel milk and its processed products would have a significant economic impact on the people living in ASALs.
Camel milk is known to have a significant impact on pastoral capacities to cope and adapt to change. It represents a major source of income for pastoralist inhabiting in drylands of Africa, and Asia (including India). It is important to note that pastoral communities in Kenya are one of the most marginalized and impoverished groups. Moreover, they are disproportionately impacted by increased climate variability due to their dependence on forage, feed and other natural resources.

agency: Department for Business, Energy and Industrial Strategy
titles: Temophadis International Enterprise and University of Lincoln
descriptions:
To develop & implement food processing techniques achieving commercially viable value added products with improved nutritional quality, increased food security & reducing 50% food losses incurred in Nigeria; Improve supply of foods via e-platforms; Build the capacity of ‘Agri-food’ vendors in Nigeria.
Innovation area – Food processing / nutrition
Some of the challenges in Nigeria are lack of knowledge of nutritional and allergen information, packaging options (like biodegradable packaging) and traceability (local foods and recipes). The KTP will help address these challenges as well as advance the TIE business as these capabilities are currently out of our reach. The KTP will particularly support TIE in the following areas where we lack knowledge / capability;
- Food product formulation and development
- Processing options to diversify offering and secure commercially viable shelf life
- Batch recipe and traceability management (including inks to a recall system)
- Current practices and technology in packaging
- Clean labelling (removal of additives / e-numbers) and development of a database on portion size conversion
- Flavour interaction, organoleptic performance, and food chemistry
- Record keeping, documentations and benchmarking
- Demand and supply chain management
- Supply chain visibility, traceability and marketing
ODA – The KTP will address food waste and increase food options by processing food crops into more shelf-stable nutritious products. Our vision is to develop socially responsible business growth models which enhance the levels of nutritious food supply in Nigeria, reducing malnutrition, food waste and insecurity.
The initiative proposed will enhance the Nigerian food supply chain by extending collaborative / cooperative networks using the company’s e-platform as a key tool for engagement and communication. These objectives will dovetail into reducing food crop losses and waste, increasing income for the farmers and others within the food value and supply chains through increased economic activities, enhancing households’ livelihood and reducing poverty levels.

agency: Department for Business, Energy and Industrial Strategy
titles: Development and assessment of nematode resistant potato cultivars for East Africa (Kenya)
descriptions: Potato is the second most important crop in Kenya and is grown for food and as a source of income. The vast majority of growers in Kenya are smallholder farmers. Pests and diseases cause huge losses to crop production across the world, including Kenya. Potato production in Kenya is being seriously impacted by an emerging introduced pathogen, the Potato Cyst Nematode (PCN).

agency: Department for Business, Energy and Industrial Strategy
titles: Design and development of direct-coupled photovoltaic powered agri-processing machinery
descriptions: Solar PV technology has seen the highest growth rate among all renewable energy resources in the last decade and a steep learning curve resulting in a significant reduction in the cost of key components such as solar modules. For example, in the last decade, the price of solar modules has reduced ten times. In such a scenario developing solar PV agricultural processing machines is a rewarding proposition, particularly in the geographic south, notably Africa has an added advantage in terms of total solar radiations received.

agency: Department for Business, Energy and Industrial Strategy
titles: Novel plant-growth-promoting rhizobacteria for improved cultivation and nutrition of maize crops
descriptions: There is a need for a balanced approach to addressing growing world food demands and meeting the green standards set by the various regulatory bodies. One of these standards is the use of alternatives to chemical fertilizers. The African Centre for Gene Technologies (ACGT) has strong experience in establishing and managing collaborative programmes in the field of biotechnology. The ACGT will be coordinating and facilitating a collaborative project between Omnia, a South African biotechnology company and domain experts from the University of Edinburgh.

agency: Department for Business, Energy and Industrial Strategy
titles: Bringing affordable soil testing to smallholder farmers in sub-Saharan Africa
descriptions: Food demand in Sub-Saharan Africa is projected to triple between 2010 and 2050 and rapid closure of the gap between current farm yields and yield potential is needed to maintain the current level of cereal self-sufficiency (approximately 80%) by 2050. Without it, the result will be massive cropland expansion with attendant biodiversity loss and greenhouse gas emissions or vast import dependency.

agency: Department for Business, Energy and Industrial Strategy
titles: Cost-effective aquaponic solutions for developing farmers in Rwanda.
descriptions: In Rwanda, 1million+ smallholder farmers who wish to provide a nutritious protein and plant-based diet while increasing yields to support economic growth are limited by: high capital costs for high yield solutions, basic farming techniques, lack of food security and consistent rainfall, few routes to market, and a dependency trap reliant on other solutions. NjordFrey (NF), offers these farmers access to sustainably designed aquaponic starter kits via an outgrower model, seasonal input product lines (e.g. seeds & fingerlings), operational training to become independent, and facilitate routes to market.

agency: Department for Business, Energy and Industrial Strategy
titles: Diagnostic tool for the identification and quantification of Potato Cyst Nematode (PCN)
descriptions: Globally, potato has proved a valuable and nutritious staple crop driving both food security and GDP growth. In Kenya, potato ranks second in importance, after maize, and approximately 800,000 people benefit directly from potato production. However, to date, there are several challenges facing potato production, including potato cyst nematode (PCN). PCN are tiny cysts containing hundreds of eggs that hatch into juvenile nematodes that attack roots, causing up to 80% yield loss. A recent survey in Kenya showed that PCN is widespread in the main potato growing areas, so potato farmers urgently need better diagnostic tools to detect and quantify PCN.
